data_sources: pcb-flex-cuts-explained.mdx § 'What is actually being cut' — 'The manufacturer routes two slots that nearly meet around a switch's mounting holes, leaving a narrow bridge of PCB material connecting the switch position to the rest of the board. Press the key, and that bridge — not the whole board — is what flexes.'

pcb-flex-cuts-explained.mdx § 'What the cut trades away' — 'The slot ends are stress concentrators. Wherever a routed cut terminates, the material around that point sees load funneled into a smaller cross-section than the surrounding board, and that geometry is the textbook setup for fatigue cracking under cyclic loading.'
background: transparent, matches hero-art/pcb-flex-cuts-explained.svg and hero-art/leaf-spring-mount-deep-dive.svg family
subject: Top-down crop of a PCB switch position: one large mounting hole with two small pin holes at center, encircled by two curved routed slots (annular sectors around the hole) that nearly meet — a 4-degree unlabeled gap at the top, a 30-degree bridge gap at the bottom. The bridge gap is filled with a muted-terracotta wedge. The two slot ends flanking that bridge are marked with caution-red circles and a shared 'stress concentration' label. A downward arrow above the hole marks the keystroke deflection direction.
